Sport · Society · Aichi-Nagoya 2026

The medal table was not the biggest number.

Japan’s first Asian Para Games closes today after 492 medal events. The figure that explains the week better may be 12: the years wheelchair rugby had been missing from this stage.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 24, 2026 at 09:20 JST · 9 min read

At Nagoya City Mizuho Athletic Stadium tonight, a flame will go out and the fifth Asian Para Games will close. Medal tables will offer the cleanest summary: rows of countries, columns of gold, silver and bronze. They are useful. They are also too small for what has happened across Aichi and nearby venues since October 18.

This was the first Asian Para Games held in Japan. The International Paralympic Committee says roughly 4,000 athletes and officials from 45 National Paralympic Committees were welcomed at the opening ceremony. Across seven days, 492 medal events were scheduled in 18 Para sports. The scale makes it the largest multi-Para-sport event of 2026.

45National Paralympic Committees
492medal events across 18 sports
452people in Japan’s delegation

But the number that changes the meaning of the programme is 12. Wheelchair rugby returned to the Asian Para Games after a twelve-year absence. Its last appearance was Incheon 2014. That return matters especially in Japan, whose team won Paralympic gold in Paris in 2024 and whose opening-ceremony flagbearer Katsuya Hashimoto entered the stadium representing the sport.

The surprise is not that a large event produced hundreds of medals. It is that the programme itself can erase a sport for three editions, then restore a route by which athletes, audiences and national programmes become visible.

A home delegation larger than 450

Japan’s Paralympic Committee listed 283 athletes, 15 competition partners, 131 coaches and staff, and 23 headquarters officials as of October 14: 452 people in all. Competition partners are not a footnote. In sports such as blind football and some athletics events, guides and other partners are part of how performance is made possible.

The roster also turns “disability sport” from one category into many different rule systems. Archery, athletics, badminton, blind football, boccia, cycling, goalball, judo, powerlifting, shooting, sitting volleyball, swimming and taekwondo demand different skills and classifications. The programme included sports built around precision, speed, endurance, strength, tactics and contact.

Classification is often the least understood part for a new viewer. Its purpose is not to rank the severity of a disability. It groups athletes according to how an eligible impairment affects performance in a particular sport. The same athlete may not fit the same logic in another sport because each activity asks different things of a body.

The programme changed while people watched

Wheelchair rugby was not the only structural change. Para powerlifting introduced team events at these Games. The final day includes the mixed team event after men’s and women’s team competitions on October 23. Japan entered both the men’s and mixed fields, according to World Para Powerlifting’s official preview.

Team formats alter the emotional grammar of a sport usually presented as one athlete, one bar and three attempts. Strategy expands beyond the heaviest successful lift. Selection order, consistency and combined performance give teammates a reason to watch every attempt as part of a shared score.

The official schedule also shows how the Games spread beyond a single arena. Para archery’s final sessions took place at Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park; powerlifting ran at the Nagoya City Trade and Industry Center. The event belonged to a region rather than one stadium, even though Mizuho provided the ceremonial image.

A ceremony made from local clay

The opening ceremony told its story through an owl named Konoha and her friend Mori, with performances drawing on Japanese fire festivals. Emperor Naruhito declared the Games open. Three Paralympians—Momoka Muraoka, Maya Nakanishi and Katsumi Miyake—lit a cauldron made with clay from three pottery regions in Aichi.

That cauldron compressed a local industrial history into an object meant for television. Aichi is not only the home of Toyota and advanced manufacturing. Its ceramic lineages include Seto and Tokoname, names that have travelled through Japanese language as well as trade. The flame sat in material tied to the host region long before modern international sport existed.

Official opening-ceremony stream linked by Para Support and the event. It shows the actual Games; playback availability is controlled by the official channel.

The teenager who returned to a stage

Saki Miura, who played Konoha, supplied another kind of return. According to the IPC, she was the only child from Aichi selected through auditions for the Tokyo 2020 Paralympic opening ceremony when she was in second grade. COVID-19 prevented her from taking part. In Nagoya, she performed the role, stood from her wheelchair and walked with a cane in the finale.

That moment can be read too easily as a generic “overcoming” story. Its sharper meaning is about access to the stage itself. Miura had earned a place years earlier; the pandemic removed the opportunity. Aichi-Nagoya did not manufacture her ambition. It finally gave it a public setting.

What remains after tonight

A closing ceremony cannot answer whether venues stay accessible, whether schoolchildren continue to encounter Para sport, or whether broadcasters carry these competitions between major Games. Those are longer tests. The official slogan, “Imagine One Heart,” becomes meaningful only if spectatorship changes ordinary institutions.

There is a practical media lesson here. Multi-sport events concentrate attention because schedules, results and pictures arrive together. When the event ends, each sport returns to a separate federation calendar that is harder for casual viewers to follow. Maintaining interest requires more than a commemorative highlight reel: it requires discoverable schedules, accessible venues, reliable streams and reporting that names athletes rather than treating disability itself as the story.

The host region will also be judged by ordinary journeys. A stadium can meet accessibility rules while the trip from a station, the hotel room, the restaurant entrance or an online ticket flow still creates friction. Visitors experience those systems as one route, not as separate administrative responsibilities. The Games brought thousands of people through that route at once, creating a rare stress test whose lessons should outlast the accreditation signs.

There is also an accounting lesson in the difference between participants and medal events. Four hundred ninety-two finals do not mean 492 identical opportunities: team sizes, classification categories and the number of events available vary widely by sport. Medal totals are therefore a record of competition, not a neutral measurement of how much a nation invested in every athlete. A country can climb the table by strength in event-rich sports while another builds a smaller programme around fewer medal chances.

None of that diminishes a medal. It clarifies what the table can and cannot say. Results tell us who performed best under the rules on the day. They cannot, alone, describe whether a sport had a route into schools, whether an athlete could train full time, or whether a returning discipline will remain on the next programme.

The Japanese word kyōsei—共生—appears often in public discussion around disability. It means living together or coexistence: 共 is “together,” and 生 is “life” or “to live.” It is an aspiration, not proof that barriers have disappeared. A week of sport can make excellence visible; it cannot substitute for transport, employment, education and media access.

That is why the programme’s less glamorous numbers matter. Forty-five delegations mean encounters across a vast region. Eighteen sports mean multiple ideas of athletic excellence. A twelve-year return means inclusion can be lost and rebuilt. And 452 people in the host delegation show how many roles stand behind the word “team.”

When the flame goes dark, the medal table will remain. The better question is whether the routes opened this week remain open too.
